sec.t:
The idea behind the camera is very old. Thinkers in [[@ancient-china|ancient China]] noticed that light through a small hole makes an upside-down picture. Around 1000 CE, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham, working in [[@world-cairo|Cairo]], explained why. Artists later used darkened boxes with [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]], called a camera obscura, [[@latin-roots|Latin for "dark room"]], to help them draw.

What they could not do was keep the picture. When you closed the box, it was gone.

Around 1826 or 1827, Niépce pointed a camera out of an upstairs window at his country house in France. Inside was a metal plate coated with bitumen, a tar that hardens where light hits it. After a very long exposure, at least many hours, he washed away the soft, unlit parts. What remained was a blurry image of rooftops and a courtyard.

That plate still exists. It is kept at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin, in the United States.

Photography arrived in India within a few years of its invention. Studios opened in Bombay, Calcutta and Madras, and photographers travelled to record temples, mountains and cities.

One of the most famous was Lala Deen Dayal, born in 1844. He photographed palaces, railways and royal events, and became court photographer to the [[@princely-states|Nizam]] of [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]]. Thousands of his glass plates survive and give a detailed picture of India in the late 1800s.

Early photography needed heavy equipment and chemistry. In 1888, George Eastman in the United States sold the first Kodak camera, already loaded with film for 100 pictures. When it was full, you posted the whole camera back to the company, which developed the photos and reloaded it. Its slogan was "You press the button, we do the rest." In 1900, Kodak's Brownie camera cost just one dollar.

In 1975, a Kodak engineer named Steven Sasson built the first digital camera. It weighed about 3.6 kg, took 23 seconds to record one black-and-white picture onto a cassette tape, and the picture had just 10,000 [[@pixels|pixels]]. Today a [[@cameras-phones|phone camera]] takes millions of pixels in a fraction of a second.

text: Weather forecasting starts with measurements. Every day, thousands of weather stations, [[@weather-balloons|weather balloons]], ships, aircraft, radars and satellites record temperature, air pressure, humidity and wind all over the planet. These readings are fed into some of the most powerful computers on Earth.

The computers then split the atmosphere into millions of imaginary boxes, stacked in layers from the ground up into the sky. Using the laws of physics, they calculate how the air in each box will change: warming, cooling, moving, rising, dropping rain. They step forward a few minutes at a time, again and again, until they reach days ahead. Forecasters study the results and turn them into the forecast you see.

It will rain for 40 percent of the day
40 percent of the town will get wet

st.reveal: It means that on days with weather like this, rain falls at a given spot about 4 times out of 10. So it might rain, it might not. Many forecasts come from running the computer model dozens of times and counting how many runs show rain.

Each evening, write down what actually happened. At the end, count how often the forecast was right. Was it better at predicting temperature or rain?

It means there is about a 4 in 10 chance that measurable rain will fall at any particular place in the forecast area during that time.

sec.t:
The idea came long before computers. During the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], a British scientist named Lewis Fry Richardson worked as an ambulance driver in France. In his spare time, he tried to forecast the weather using the laws of physics and a lot of arithmetic. He spent weeks calculating a forecast for just six hours ahead. The answer was badly wrong, mainly because of problems with his starting data.

In 1922 he published his method and described a dream. In a vast hall, about 64,000 people with pencils would each calculate one small patch of the atmosphere, guided by a conductor in the centre. It was never built. But his method was right.

The atmosphere is chaotic. Tiny differences at the start can grow into big differences days later. In the 1960s, the American meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered this when a small rounding of numbers in his computer model produced completely different weather later in the run. This became known as the butterfly effect, from his famous question about whether a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas.

To deal with this, forecasters run their models many times, each starting with slightly different numbers. If most runs agree, they are confident. If the runs spread out, the forecast is uncertain. Counting how many runs show rain gives you a percentage, like "70 percent chance of rain". Beyond about ten days, the runs usually disagree too much to be useful for daily weather.

Better forecasts matter most when danger is coming. In October 1999, a [[@cyclones-india|super cyclone]] struck [[@odisha|Odisha]], and around 10,000 people died. In October 2013, Cyclone Phailin, nearly as strong, hit the same coast. This time, the India Meteorological Department tracked it days in advance, and officials moved around a million people into shelters. The death toll was a small fraction of 1999's.

In the United States, forecasts of [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] give coastal towns days of warning. New tools are arriving too. In recent years, artificial intelligence models trained on decades of past weather have started making forecasts that rival traditional ones, in a fraction of the time.

text: Nelson Mandela was a South African lawyer and leader who fought against [[@apartheid|apartheid]], a system of laws that kept people apart by race and gave white South Africans power over everyone else.

For this, he spent 27 years in prison. When he was released in 1990, he worked with the government to end apartheid peacefully. In 1994, South Africa held its first election in which people of all races could vote, and Mandela became its first Black president. Instead of seeking revenge, he tried to bring the country together. People around the world still call him by his clan name, Madiba.

st.reveal: Rugby had long been seen as a white South African's sport, and many Black South Africans used to cheer against the Springboks. Mandela's choice to wear their green jersey and cap was a powerful sign that the team now belonged to everyone. South Africa won.

myth: Mandela was always committed to completely peaceful protest, just like Gandhi.

Mandela began with peaceful protest, but after police killed protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, he helped start an armed wing of the ANC. He explained this choice at his trial. In later life he worked hard for peace and reconciliation.

sec.t:
Mandela was born in 1918 in the village of Mvezo, in the Eastern Cape. His family belonged to the Thembu royal house of the Xhosa people. As a boy he herded cattle and listened to elders tell stories of his people's history.

He studied at mission schools, then at university, and moved to Johannesburg. In 1952 he and his friend Oliver Tambo opened South Africa's first Black-run law firm. Queues of people waited outside for help with the unfair laws.

From 1948, South Africa's government passed laws enforcing apartheid, meaning "apartness" in Afrikaans. People were sorted by race. Black South Africans, most of the population, could not vote, had to carry passes, and were forced to live in separate areas. Schools, hospitals, beaches and even park benches were divided.

Mandela joined the African National Congress (ANC), which campaigned against these laws. At first it used peaceful protest, strikes and boycotts.

In 1960, police shot dead 69 protesters at Sharpeville, and the ANC was banned. Mandela decided peaceful methods alone could not win and helped start an armed group that sabotaged government targets. Some people criticised this then and still do. The US government kept him on a terrorism watch list until 2008.

Mandela was arrested and, in 1964, sentenced to life in prison. At his trial he said he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free society where everyone lived together in harmony.

He spent 18 years on Robben Island, off [[@world-cape-town|Cape Town]]. Prisoners broke rocks in a limestone quarry, where the glare damaged Mandela's eyes. He slept on a mat in a tiny cell. Even so, prisoners taught each other, and the island became known as "the university".

Around the world, people campaigned for his release. Musicians sang about him, and countries refused to trade or play sport with South Africa. The island is now a museum and a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]].

{{story:unesco-sites}}

On 11 February 1990, Mandela walked out of prison, holding his wife Winnie's hand, as crowds cheered. He and President F.W. de Klerk negotiated an end to apartheid, and both won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 1993.

On 27 April 1994, millions of South Africans queued for hours to vote, many for the first time. Mandela became president. He set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, where people could tell what had happened under apartheid. He served one term, then stepped down.

Mandela often spoke of [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], who had spent 21 years in South Africa as a young lawyer and first developed his methods of protest there. India was among the first countries to cut trade with apartheid South Africa, in 1946.

India gave Mandela the Bharat Ratna in 1990, soon after his release. Since 2010, 18 July, his birthday, has been marked worldwide as Nelson Mandela International Day. People are asked to spend 67 minutes helping others, one minute for every year he spent working for change.

text: In 1857, Indian soldiers in the army of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] rose up against their British officers. The revolt began at Meerut on 10 May and spread quickly across north and central India.

Rebel soldiers marched to [[@delhi|Delhi]] and declared the elderly Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, their leader. Kings, queens, landlords, farmers and townspeople joined in many places. Leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Begum Hazrat Mahal of Lucknow, Nana Sahib of Kanpur, Tatya Tope and Kunwar Singh of Bihar. The fighting was fierce, with terrible killings on both sides. By mid-1858 the British had crushed the revolt. The Company lost control of India, and the British Crown took over.

st.reveal: Soldiers had to bite open the paper cartridges. Rumours spread that the grease contained beef fat, offensive to Hindus, and pork fat, offensive to Muslims. The British changed the rules, but by then trust had broken down.

The cartridges were the spark. Underneath were years of anger about kingdoms taken over by the British, heavy land taxes, low pay for soldiers and fears that the British wanted to change Indians' religions and customs.

sec.t:
In early 1857, British officials noticed something odd. Village watchmen were receiving chapatis from a nearby village, with instructions to make more and pass them on. Thousands of [[@roti-chapati|chapatis]] travelled hundreds of kilometres this way.

Nobody could explain it. The British feared it was a secret signal for rebellion. Some villagers seem to have thought it was a charm against disease. Historians still don't know what it meant, but it shows how tense and uneasy north India was.

The cartridges lit a fire that had long been ready to burn. The Company had taken over kingdoms such as Awadh in 1856, and Jhansi and others under a rule called the Doctrine of Lapse. Rulers, nobles and their soldiers lost status.

Farmers faced high land taxes. Many Indians feared British laws and missionaries were attacking their religion and customs. Sepoys were paid much less than British soldiers and could rarely be promoted. So when the revolt began, many groups had reasons of their own to join.

Delhi was held by the rebels for four months. In September 1857, British forces stormed the city after a long siege. Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, and two of his sons and a grandson were shot.

At Kanpur, British men, women and children were killed after surrendering. British troops took brutal revenge in many towns, hanging villagers and blowing rebels from cannons. At Lucknow, British families held out in the Residency for months. The ruined Residency still stands, its walls marked by cannonballs.

In 1858, Parliament ended the Company's rule, and Queen Victoria became ruler of India. Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, ending the [[@mughals|Mughal]] line.

The British reorganised the army and became more careful about interfering with religion. Indians remembered 1857 in many ways. In 1909, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar called it the First War of Indian Independence, and the name spread. In 2007, India marked 150 years since the revolt with events across the country.

text: The Stone Age is the long stretch of time when people made their tools mainly from stone. It began more than 3 million years ago and lasted until metal tools spread, which happened at different times in different places. For most of it, people lived by hunting animals, fishing and gathering plants, nuts, fruit, roots and honey.

They usually lived in small groups of a few families, perhaps 20 to 50 people. Groups moved with the seasons, following animals and ripening plants. They knew their land in great detail: which berries were safe, where water stayed in the dry season, and when fish would swim upriver.

About 6 hours
About half the day

st.reveal: Stone tools go back about 3.3 million years, and farming began about 12,000 years ago. 12,000 divided by 3.3 million, times 24 hours, comes to roughly 5 minutes. Almost all of the human story happened before anyone planted a seed.

Most people lived in the open, in huts or tents made of wood, hides, grass and even mammoth bones. Caves are simply good at preserving tools and paintings, so they are where many finds turn up.

sec.t:
Stone does not rot, so tools are the clues archaeologists find most. The earliest were simple: a stone struck to make a sharp edge for cutting meat. Later, around 1.7 million years ago, people began shaping hand axes, teardrop-shaped tools that fit the palm. They were made the same careful way for over a million years.

India has some of the oldest. At Attirampakkam, near [[@chennai|Chennai]], researchers found hand axes about 1.5 million years old. Over time, tools grew smaller and smarter: blades, spear points, bone needles with eyes for thread, and fish hooks.

Wood, leather, string and baskets were probably just as important, but most of them rotted away long ago.

A day might mean gathering plants and small animals near camp, while others went hunting or fishing. Food was shared. Studies of people who still hunt and gather suggest they often worked fewer hours on food than many farmers later did, though life could be hard in bad seasons.

[[@fire-discovery|Fire]] changed everything. It gave warmth, light, protection from animals and cooked food, which is easier to chew and digest. Evenings round a fire were a time to talk, tell stories and teach children.

People also made beautiful things. They wore shell beads, carved figures from bone and ivory, and painted animals on rock walls.

{{story:cave-art}}

For much of the last 2 million years, Earth swung in and out of [[@ice-ages|ice ages]]. In Europe and northern Asia, people hunted reindeer, horses and woolly [[@mammoths|mammoths]]. They sewed fitted clothes with bone needles and built shelters from mammoth bones and hides.

As people spread out of Africa, they reached Asia, [[@australia|Australia]] and finally the Americas. Many scientists think people reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago, and some think earlier. About 13,000 years ago, hunters across North America made a distinctive stone spear tip now called the Clovis point.

sec.h: Bhimbetka: a home for thousands of years
sec.t:
In [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], about 45 km from Bhopal, a cluster of rock shelters called [[@art-cave-paintings-bhimbetka|Bhimbetka]] was used by people for many thousands of years. Its walls carry hundreds of paintings in red and white: hunters, dancers, deer, bison and elephants. Some are thought to be about 10,000 years old, and others were painted much later.

In 1957 an archaeologist named V.S. Wakankar spotted the rocks from a train window and guessed they might hold old sites. He was right. Bhimbetka became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 2003.

sec.h: The end of the Stone Age
sec.t: About 12,000 years ago, some groups began to plant seeds and keep animals. [[@farming-began|Farming]] led to villages, then towns. Copper, then bronze and iron, slowly replaced stone. But the Stone Age did not end because people ran out of stones. It ended because they found something new to try.

text: Arizona is a state in the south-west of the USA, next to Mexico. It became the 48th state in 1912, the last of the 48 states that touch each other on the map. Much of the south is the Sonoran Desert, home to giant saguaro cactuses and summer days that can pass 45°C in the capital, Phoenix.

But Arizona is not all low desert. The north is a high plateau with pine forests, snow and the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]], carved by the Colorado River. The state is also home to 22 Native American tribes, including the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo Nation]], the biggest reservation in the country. Arizona packs deserts, mountains, canyons and dark starry skies into one state a little smaller than Rajasthan.

st.prompt: A saguaro cactus usually grows its first arm when it is how old?

options.t: About 2 years
About 10 years
Somewhere around 50 to 70 years

st.reveal: Saguaros grow very slowly. A ten-year-old plant may be only a few centimetres tall, and the first arms usually appear after half a century or more, depending on rain. Some saguaros live for over 150 years.

myth: Deserts like Arizona are always hot.
Arizona's high country gets real winters. Flagstaff, at over 2,100 m, is one of the snowiest cities in the USA, and the rim of the Grand Canyon is often white in January.

sec.t:
The saguaro (say "sa-WAH-ro") grows wild only in the Sonoran Desert, in Arizona and north-western Mexico. A big one can be 12 metres tall, as high as a four-storey building, and weigh several tonnes when full of water. One heavy rain can let it soak up hundreds of litres through roots that spread out just under the surface.

Woodpeckers drill nest holes in the trunk. Later, tiny [[@owl-eyes|elf owls]] move into the empty holes. In late spring, white flowers open at night on the tips of the arms, and bats, [[@pollinators|bees]] and doves drink their [[nectar|nectar]]. The Tohono O'odham people have long harvested the red fruit to make syrup and jam.

sec.h: Dark skies and a lost planet
sec.t:
In 1930, a young astronomer named Clyde Tombaugh was working at Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff. He compared photos of the same patch of sky taken nights apart, looking for a dot that moved. He found one: [[@pluto|Pluto]].

Flagstaff has worked hard to keep its skies dark, with rules about outdoor lights. In 2001 it became the first International Dark Sky City. On a clear night there, the [[@stargazing|Milky Way]] stretches across the sky like a pale cloud.

Arizonans once spoke of the "five Cs" that built the state: copper, cattle, cotton, citrus and climate. Copper still matters. Arizona mines around two-thirds of all the copper produced in the USA, metal that ends up in wires, pipes and phones.

Water is the thing Arizona never has enough of. Phoenix gets only about 20 cm of rain a year, less than Mumbai can get in a single wet day. So a concrete canal more than 500 km long, the Central Arizona Project, carries water from the Colorado River across the desert to Phoenix and Tucson. As the river shrinks in long droughts, the state has had to cut back on how much it takes.

Then there are the clocks. Summer days in Phoenix are hot enough without an extra hour of evening sun, so in 1968 the state chose to skip daylight saving time. The Navajo Nation, which spreads into Utah and New Mexico, does change its clocks. Inside it lies the Hopi reservation, which doesn't. Drive across the north-east of the state in summer and your phone may change its mind several times.

text: Himachal Pradesh is a mountain state in northern India, stretching from green, forested foothills up to snowy peaks and the high, dry valleys of [[@spiti|Lahaul and Spiti]]. Most people live in small towns and villages on slopes, often in houses of stone and wood with slate roofs that shed the snow.

Life follows the seasons and the steep land. Families grow apples, plums and potatoes on terraces cut into the hills. Roads twist in hairpin bends. Winter brings snow to many places, while summer brings visitors escaping the heat of the plains. Many villages have their own local deity, and festivals like Kullu Dussehra fill whole valleys with music.

st.prompt: Every summer in British times, the whole government of India moved somewhere. Where did it go?

Down to the beaches of Goa
Across to Kolkata by river

st.reveal: From 1864, the British government moved to Shimla each summer to escape the heat of the plains. Officials, clerks and files all travelled up the mountain, and Shimla became the "summer capital".

myth: The hill states of India are cold everywhere all year.
Himachal ranges from warm valleys about 350 m above sea level to icy passes above 5,000 m. Lower towns can be hot in summer, while high places like Spiti stay cold and dry most of the year.

sec.t:
The British found Shimla's cool air a relief from the scorching plains. From 1864, the government of British India moved there every summer, carrying files, clerks and officials up the mountain. Shimla filled with churches, mock-Tudor buildings and a long promenade called the Mall.

To get there more easily, they built the [[@india-wonder-toy-train|Kalka–Shimla Railway]], which opened in 1903. Its tiny trains run on narrow tracks about 96 km through 102 tunnels and over hundreds of bridges, climbing well over a kilometre in height. In 2008, it was added to UNESCO's list of the Mountain Railways of India, alongside the Darjeeling and Nilgiri lines.

North of the high Rohtang Pass lie Lahaul and Spiti, where the land changes completely. Very little rain gets over the mountains, so the valleys are dry, rocky and brown. Spiti looks more like [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] or Tibet than the green hills near Shimla.

Villages there are some of the highest lived-in places in India. Old Buddhist monasteries, such as Key and Tabo, cling to the hillsides. Tabo's monastery was founded in 996 and still holds ancient paintings. Snow leopards, ibex and blue sheep live on the high slopes. Farmers here grow barley and green peas in the short summer, watering their fields with channels of melted snow.

For centuries, the Rohtang Pass closed with snow for months each winter. In 2020, the [[@india-wonder-atal-tunnel|Atal Tunnel]] opened beneath it, about 9 km long, so Lahaul now stays connected all year.

Steep slopes and heavy monsoon rain make [[@landslides|landslides]] a real danger. In recent years, floods and slides have washed away roads, bridges and buildings, especially in 2023. Scientists say that building on fragile slopes, cutting forests and changing rainfall patterns all play a part.

Dharamshala, another hill town, has a different story. Since 1960, the Dalai Lama, the Tibetan Buddhist leader, has lived in McLeod Ganj just above it, and many Tibetans have settled there. On a clear day, visitors can watch monks debating in a courtyard while the snowy Dhauladhar range glows behind them.

text: Peru is a country on the Pacific coast of South America. Few countries pack in such different lands. A narrow desert runs along the coast, where it hardly ever rains. Behind it rise the Andes, with peaks over 6,000 metres. On the far side, the mountains drop into the Amazon rainforest, which covers more than half of Peru.

Peru was the heart of the Inca Empire, the largest empire in the Americas before Europeans arrived. It is known for Machu Picchu, the mysterious [[@mystery-nazca-lines|Nazca Lines]], llamas and alpacas, and the potato. Many people still speak Quechua, the language of the Inca, alongside [[@spanish-language|Spanish]]. In the misty cloud forests lives the spectacled bear, the only bear in South America. Paddington Bear, in the children's books, comes from "darkest Peru".

st.prompt: The Nazca Lines are giant drawings scratched into the desert of southern Peru. Where do you have to be to see them properly?

options.t: Up in the air, or on a nearby hill
Standing in the middle of one
Underground

st.reveal: The figures are so big that from the ground they just look like shallow paths. The hummingbird alone is about 93 metres long, nearly as long as a football field. They are best seen from a small plane or from viewing towers and hills nearby.

Local farmers knew about Machu Picchu, and some were living and farming on its terraces. A local man guided Bingham there. Bingham's photographs made the site famous around the world.

sec.t:
[[@inca-machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]] sits on a ridge high above a river gorge, about 2,400 metres up. It was built around 1450, probably as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti. Its stone walls fit together so tightly, with no mortar, that you cannot slide a knife blade between the blocks. That tight fit helps them survive earthquakes.

The Inca left it about a century later. Spanish soldiers never found it, so it was not destroyed. In 1911, the American explorer Hiram Bingham was led there by local people, and his photographs made it world famous. Today visitor numbers are limited to protect it.

Farmers in the Andes around Lake Titicaca tamed the wild [[@potatoes|potato]] roughly 8,000 years ago. Andean families still grow thousands of kinds, in purple, red, yellow and blue, some knobbly, some long and thin. The International Potato Center in Lima keeps a seed bank of thousands of varieties so they will never be lost.

Andean farmers also invented a way to freeze-dry potatoes. They leave them out on frosty nights, let them thaw in the sun, then squash out the water by treading on them. The dried result, chuño, can be stored for years. The Spanish took potatoes to Europe in the 1500s, and from there they spread to India and the rest of the world.

On the dry plains near Nazca, people living about 2,000 years ago scraped away dark stones to reveal pale ground beneath. They made straight lines kilometres long and huge pictures of a monkey, a spider and a [[@hummingbirds|hummingbird]]. Because it barely rains or blows hard there, the lines have survived for centuries.

Nobody knows for sure why they were made. They may have been paths walked in ceremonies, perhaps linked to water, the most precious thing in a desert.

text: Monument Valley is a stretch of red desert on the border of Arizona and Utah, in the southwestern USA. Huge rock towers rise from the flat sand, some about 300 m tall, as high as a 90-storey building. Geologists call the flat-topped ones mesas and buttes, and the thin ones spires.

The valley lies inside the Navajo Nation, the largest Native American reservation in the USA. The Navajo call it Tsé Biiʼ Ndzisgaii, which means roughly "valley of the rocks". It became famous around the world as the backdrop of old cowboy films, but for the Navajo it has always been home.

st.prompt: Why are Monument Valley's towers so red?

Red sand blows onto them from far away
Desert sunsets have stained them over time

st.reveal: The sandstone contains tiny amounts of iron. Over time, the iron has reacted with oxygen to form iron oxide, which is basically rust. A small amount is enough to paint the whole landscape red.

d.try: Build a mini butte. Pack damp sand into a cup, turn it out on a tray, and press a flat stone or a coin on top. Pour water gently over it from a cup held above. Watch the unprotected sand wash away while the part under the stone survives, just like a butte with its hard cap.
myth: Monument Valley's rocks were carved by one giant flood.

They were shaped slowly over millions of years. Rain, frost and wind wore away softer rock, while harder layers on top protected the towers beneath them. The process is still going on, a grain at a time.

sec.t:
The towers are made mostly of sandstone, rock formed from sand pressed and cemented together. Much of it was laid down about 270 million years ago, as dunes and river sand, long before the first dinosaurs. The sandstone is red because tiny bits of iron in it have rusted.

On top of many towers sits a thinner layer of harder rock. That cap acts like a lid. It protects the softer sandstone underneath from rain and wind, as described in the story of how [[@rocks-types|rocks form]].

Millions of years ago, this whole area was a flat, high plateau. Rain, frost and wind began cutting cracks into it. Water widened the cracks into gullies, and the gullies grew into valleys.

What was left formed a kind of ladder. A large flat block is a mesa. When erosion shrinks a mesa until it is taller than it is wide, it is called a butte. When a butte wears down to a thin finger, it is a spire. One day, each spire will tumble too. The same slow forces of water and weather explain how [[@cliffs-erosion|cliffs erode]] everywhere.

sec.h: Shadows, mittens and a totem pole

sec.t:
In 1939, director John Ford filmed Stagecoach here, starring John Wayne. He returned for many more westerns. For millions of people, Monument Valley became the picture of the American West. Many local Navajo people worked on the films as actors, guides and helpers.

Later films went there too. In Forrest Gump (1994), the hero ends his years-long run across America on a road with the towers behind him. That stretch of US Route 163 is now one of the most photographed roads in the country. Visitors often stand in the middle of it, which is dangerous because cars still use it.

The Navajo Nation covers about 71,000 km² across Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. That is larger than the Indian state of Punjab. In 1958 the Navajo opened Monument Valley as a tribal park, which they still run.

Visitors can drive a dirt loop past many of the buttes. To go deeper into the valley, they must hire a Navajo guide. Some families still live there without mains electricity, herding sheep and weaving rugs. The Navajo language that you might hear in the valley once became an unbreakable military code, a story told in [[@code-talkers|the code talkers]].

text: Dr. Seuss was the pen name of Theodor Seuss Geisel, an American writer and cartoonist who lived from 1904 to 1991. He wrote and drew more than 60 children's books, including The Cat in the Hat, Green Eggs and Ham, How the Grinch Stole [[@christmas|Christmas]] and The Lorax.

He made reading fun by turning it into a game. His books bounce along with strong rhythm and [[@poems-for-kids|silly rhymes]]. They use simple words that new readers can sound out, and wild pictures of creatures nobody has ever seen. Children can read them alone, which feels like a superpower when you are six.

st.reveal: His publisher, Bennett Cerf, bet him 50 dollars that he couldn't write a book with only 50 different words. Seuss did it, and Green Eggs and Ham became one of the best-selling children's books in English.

d.try: Write a four-line rhyme using only words of one syllable, like "The fat cat sat on a big red hat." Then try to tell a tiny story in it. You will quickly find out why writing simple words is harder than it looks.
myth: Dr. Seuss was a real doctor.

Theodor Geisel had no medical or academic doctorate when he took the name. He used "Dr." partly as a joke for his father, who had hoped he would earn a doctorate and become a professor. Dartmouth College gave him an honorary doctorate in 1956.

sec.h: The problem with Dick and Jane
sec.t:
In the 1950s, most American children learned to read from school books about two children called Dick and Jane. The sentences went like "See Dick run. Run, Dick, run." Many children found them dull.

In 1954, the writer John Hersey wrote a magazine article asking why reading books for beginners were so boring. He suggested that someone like Dr. Seuss should write them. A publisher then gave Geisel a list of a few hundred words that young children should know, and challenged him to write a book using only those.

The result was The Cat in the Hat (1957), which uses about 236 different words. A tall cat in a striped hat turns up on a rainy day while their mother is out and wrecks the house, then tidies it all up just in time. It sold more than a million copies within a few years and changed beginner books for good.

{{story:rhythm-beat}}

sec.h: A beat you can bounce to
sec.t:
Read Seuss aloud and you can hear a steady pattern: da-da-DUM, da-da-DUM. Try "I do not like green eggs and ham. I do not like them, Sam-I-am." The [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] makes lines easy to remember and fun to say, a little like [[@tongue-twisters|tongue twisters]].

The rhymes help too. If a child can read "cat", they can guess "hat", "sat" and "that". Seuss also loved made-up words, like Sneetches, Lorax and the Grinch. Nonsense words can't be guessed from memory, so readers have to sound them out, which is exactly the practice they need.

Before he wrote for children, Geisel drew cartoons and advertisements. His first children's book, And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street (1937), was rejected by more than 20 publishers.

Many later books carry big ideas in silly packages. In The Lorax (1971), a small creature "speaks for the trees" against a businessman who chops them all down. It is still read in classrooms about [[@environment-heroes|protecting nature]]. The Sneetches is about creatures who look down on each other for not having stars on their bellies. Horton Hears a Who! says that "a person's a person, no matter how small".

Not everything Geisel drew has aged well. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], he drew political cartoons that included racist pictures of Japanese people. Some early books also contain hurtful pictures of people from Asia and Africa.

In 2021, the company that looks after his books stopped publishing six of them because of such images. Some people agreed with the decision. Others felt the books should stay in print with explanations. Either way, his most famous titles remain in shops and [[@school-history|classrooms]].

In the United States, his birthday, 2 March, is used each year to celebrate reading, with "Read Across America" events in schools.

text: A palindrome is a word, number or sentence that reads the same backwards as forwards. "Level", "radar" and "madam" are palindromes. So is the number 12321, and the date 22/02/2022.

For longer phrases, people usually ignore spaces, capital letters and [[@words-punctuation|punctuation]]. The most famous English one is "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama". The word palindrome comes from Greek words meaning "running back again".

st.reveal: Multiplying numbers made only of 1s gives a palindrome that climbs and falls. 11 × 11 = 121 and 111 × 111 = 12321. The pattern holds up to 111,111,111 × 111,111,111 = 12,345,678,987,654,321.

d.try: Pick any two-digit number, like 57. Reverse it and add, so 57 + 75 = 132. Do it again, and 132 + 231 = 363, a palindrome. Try other numbers and count how many steps each takes. Some, like 89, take a surprisingly long time.
myth: Every number becomes a palindrome if you keep reversing it and adding.
Most numbers do, but nobody has ever turned 196 into a palindrome this way, even after computers carried on for millions of steps. Nobody has proved it never will, either.
facts: the Sator square, found at Pompeii

sec.t:
English is full of short ones: noon, kayak, racecar, refer. The [[@words-longest|longest]] common English palindromes are only about seven to nine letters, like "rotator" and "rotavator". The Irish writer James Joyce invented a longer one in his 1922 novel Ulysses: "tattarrattat", the sound of someone knocking at a door. It has 12 letters, and the Oxford English Dictionary lists it.

One of the best-known palindromes in India is the name of a language: [[@malayalam|Malayalam]], spoken mostly in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. In Hindi, you can find short palindromes such as jalaj, meaning lotus, and nayan, meaning eye. They read the same both ways in Devanagari letters as well as in English spelling.

[[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poets went much further. In a style called viloma kavya, verses can be read forwards and backwards. One famous Sanskrit poem, the Ramakrishna Viloma Kavyam, tells the story of Rama when read one way and of Krishna when read the other way.

In maths, palindromic numbers have a kind of [[@symmetry|symmetry]]. 121, 1331 and 14641 are palindromes, and they are also powers of 11. Squaring numbers made only of 1s gives a beautiful pattern: 1, 121, 12321, 1234321, all the way up to 12345678987654321.

There is a game you can play with almost any number. Reverse it and add. If the answer isn't a palindrome, do it again. For 57, it takes two steps. For 89, it takes 24 steps and ends with a 13-digit number.

For 196, nobody has ever reached a palindrome, even using computers for years. Mathematicians are still unsure whether it ever will. Some people use computers to test palindromes in other [[@number-systems|number systems]], like [[@binary-code|binary]], where the patterns change completely.

Palindromes even appear in living things. [[@dna|DNA]] is made of two strands with four chemical letters: A, T, G and C. A always pairs with T, and G with C. Some short stretches read the same on one strand as on the other strand going the opposite way.

For example, GAATTC on one strand sits opposite CTTAAG, which reversed is GAATTC again. Bacteria make proteins that recognise palindromes like this and cut DNA there. Scientists borrowed those proteins as tools, and they helped make modern genetics possible.

Palindromes are a bit like word [[@riddles|riddles]]. Writers have spent years building long palindrome sentences and even whole palindrome poems, just to show it can be done.

text: Ready-to-eat food for busy people is older than most cities. Romans bought hot stews at street counters, Chinese traders slurped [[@noodles-pasta|noodles]] at market stalls, and Indian towns have had snack sellers for as long as anyone can remember.

What we now call fast food, though, took shape in the USA in the 20th century. Burger chains like White Castle, starting in 1921, and McDonald's, which reorganised its kitchen in 1948, worked out how to make the same food quickly, cheaply and identically, again and again. Cars, highways and advertising carried the idea across America, and later across the planet.

st.prompt: In 1948 the McDonald brothers changed their restaurant to make food faster. What did they do?

options.t: Cut the menu to a few items and split cooking into simple, repeated jobs
Bought robots to flip the burgers
Asked customers to cook their own food

st.reveal: They dropped carhops, plates and most of the menu. One worker grilled, one added toppings, one made shakes, one fried potatoes. Like a factory line, each person did one job very fast.

sec.t:
Long before burger chains, Indian streets were full of food made in seconds. A pani puri seller can fill and hand over a puri faster than you can eat it. Samosas, chaat and kathi rolls were all designed for eating standing up.

Mumbai's vada pav, a spicy potato fritter in a soft bun, is often called the city's burger. It is said to have been sold first by a snack seller named Ashok Vaidya near Dadar station in the 1960s, for mill workers who needed a cheap, filling lunch. [[@street-food|Street food]] like this still feeds millions of Indians every day, often faster than any chain.

In 1921, White Castle opened in Wichita, Kansas, selling small square burgers for five cents. Its owners made the kitchens spotless and open to view, to convince Americans that cheap meat could be safe.

Then, in 1948, Richard and Maurice McDonald shut their drive-in in San Bernardino, California, for a few months. They reopened with only nine items and a kitchen run like a factory. Each worker had one task. Burgers were made before anyone ordered. They called it the Speedee Service System. Henry Ford had done something similar decades earlier, when he sped up [[@cars-history|car making]] by moving each car past a line of workers who each fitted one part.

A milkshake-machine seller named Ray Kroc visited the brothers in 1954 and saw the future. He began selling franchises, letting other owners open copies of the restaurant using the same rules. He later bought the company. By the 1970s, chains such as McDonald's, KFC and Burger King were spreading around the world.

In India, the chains had to change. McDonald's opened its first Indian restaurant in Delhi in 1996 with no beef or pork. It added the McAloo Tikki burger and plenty of vegetarian choices. Domino's, [[@pizza|Pizza]] Hut and KFC adjusted too, with paneer toppings and spicier flavours.

Fast food is cheap and tasty, but much of it is high in fat, salt and sugar and low in fibre. Eating it often is linked to health problems, which is why doctors suggest keeping [[@junk-food|junk food]] as an occasional treat. Big chains have also been criticised for the waste they create and for advertising aimed at children.

Some new food businesses try to keep the speed and lose the downsides. Yet the cheapest, quickest healthy meal in Mumbai may still be the home-cooked lunch that arrives by dabbawala.
